near_miss.lead: kin series father/mother/brother in marriage-consent law (ON rað faður eða moðor eða broðor) ~ OIr legal pair list (athair frin ingin ... brathair, mac fria mathair, fer fria bein) ~ AV mātuḥ ... bhrātuḥ ... pituḥ (bride kept in the family house)
near_miss.why_not: Cognate kin terms only; enumerating father, mother, brother (and husband/wife) is universal in family law and charms. The syntax differs: ON genitive series governed by rað, OIr 'X fria Y' pairs, AV locative genitives. Nothing points to a fixed inherited order or figure.

near_miss.lead: list of marriage guardians faðer eða moðer eða broðer ~ MBh mātā pitā ca bhrātā ca bhāryā ca ~ AV mātā ... pitā ... bhrātā
near_miss.why_not: Generic kin enumeration; the order differs (ON father-mother-brother, Skt mother-father-brother); the contexts don't match (ON guardianship law, MBh list of those the king must punish, AV the kin who 'let loose' a disease).

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 579 - PDF page 59 (word id 9376)
near_miss.lead: incest catalogue: Arm. dstersk' haranc' ... k'ork' ełbarc' ... mark' ... yordwoc' (daughters to fathers, sisters to brothers, mothers to sons) ~ Eur. Andr. 174 πατήρ τε θυγατρὶ παῖς τε μητρὶ μίγνυται, κόρη τ’ ἀδελφῷ
near_miss.why_not: A striking match in content and order (father-daughter, son-mother, sister-brother, with cognate *ph2ter, *dhugh2ter, *meh2ter, *bhreh2ter), but both describe the same thing: the Iranian next-of-kin marriage that Greek writers held up as barbarian. Eghishe (5th c., Greek-educated) is drawing on the Greek ethnographic topos or on what he saw himself. This is a borrowed or independent topos, not inherited phraseology, and the kin terms are forced by the subject.

near_miss.lead: telling the tale: ON sagði sǫguna (segja + saga, both *sekw-) ~ OIr adfét scéla (scél < *sekw-tlom)
near_miss.why_not: OIr uses a different verb (ad-fét, not a reflex of *sekw-), so there is no figura etymologica in Irish; 'tell news' is everyday language in both. The *bhrew- words (brennunni / bruthmar) are unrelated in sense and context.

near_miss.lead: Rígsþula: vǫll nam at rjóða, val nam at fella
near_miss.why_not: The slab partners (OIr satire on a poet; Cato's equipment list) have nothing comparable. The real partner is outside the slab; see the search_lead line (Homeric γαῖαν ἐρεύθων).

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 597 - PDF page 77 (word id 12340)
near_miss.lead: hearts of all men, men and women: ON allra manna hiortu ... karla ok kvenna ~ Arm. mi sirt ... amenecʻown aranc' ew kananc', cerocʻ ew tłayocʻ
near_miss.why_not: Both are Christian or learned prose (Snorra Edda prologue euhemerism; Eghishe's Christian rhetoric). The 'men and women' merism and 'heart' are generic. ON karl (man) and Arm. cer (old) do not match in meaning, and karl < *ǵerh2- is uncertain.

near_miss.lead: night without sleep: ON ekki var þá óttalaust at sofa ... at miðri nótt ~ Hom. ἀΰπνους νύκτας ἴαυον
near_miss.why_not: Different expressions: 'not fearless to sleep' versus 'sleepless nights' (privative compound with the plural accusative of time). They share only *nokwt- and *swep-/*supno-, which co-occur everywhere.

near_miss.lead: nine nights without food: MidIr nái n-aidchi gan bhiadh (Goll besieged); compare Hávamál 138-9 (Óðinn's nine nights, no bread or horn) [not in slab]
near_miss.why_not: The slab partner (Vǫluspá, unsown fields shall grow) shares nothing with the Irish. 'Nine nights' is a widespread ritual and narrative number (recalled), and Goll's starving under siege is a late Fenian narrative, not a formula.

near_miss.lead: shields in battle array: EModIr sgíath breacbhuidhe ... for a mhuin ~ Igor Tale чрьлеными щиты прегородиша, ищучи себѣ чти, а князю славы
near_miss.why_not: They share only 'shield' (sciath ~ щитъ, *skeyt-). The Irish 'chlíu' is clí 'left side', not clú 'fame', so there is no 'fame' parallel to слава. The Irish is an Early Modern description of the hero's equipment.

search_lead.cognate: ON rjóða (strong verb 'redden') = Gk ἐρεύθω, aor. ἐρεῦσαι, both < *h1rewdh- 'make red'; the object 'earth/field' is renewed (ON vǫllr / fold, Gk γαῖα)
search_lead.argument: The same verb + object, 'redden the ground (with blood)', describes a warrior killing in both traditions: Rígsþula 37 (Konr ungr: hiǫrvi brá, víg nam at vekja, vǫll nam at rjóða, val nam at fella), Reginsmál 26 (sás fold ryði, of Sigurðr), and in Homer of a slain man's killer (Il. 11.394) and of Achilles and Patroclus fated to 'redden the same earth' (Il. 18.329). In both, the verb of the inherited root takes an earth noun as direct object. Caveats: 'redden the ground with blood' is natural battle imagery and could arise independently; the noun differs; ON rjóða most often takes weapons as object (geir, eggjar, sverð, odd ok egg, 19 lemma hits), so the earth object is the rarer use. The case is weak to moderate, worth a review that includes Vedic/Avestan *h1rewdh- uses.

error.correct_reading: clí 'left side, body' (dat. sg. clíu): claideamh órdhoirn for a chlíu 'a gold-hilted sword on his left side'
error.evidence: The standard equipment formula: spear(s) in hand, shield on back, sword on the left side. 'Fame' makes no sense with 'for'.

error.correct_reading: adaig 'night' (here acc. pl. after nái: nine nights); not from *h2eǵ- 'drive'
error.evidence: The context 'nái n-aidchi gan bhiadh' is nine nights without food. The verb *h2eǵ- (OIr ad-aig 'drives') is a homograph; the noun adaig 'night' has a disputed etymology unrelated to 'drive'.

error.correct_reading: do-icc/tic 'came' (3 sg. perf. táinic), a verb, not a name
error.evidence: Táinic buiden mór ... isin telaich: 'a great troop came onto the hill'.

note: Second reader on 9 flagged bundles. No claims. 9 near-misses; one search lead (ON rjóða vǫll/fold ~ Hom. γαῖαν ἐρεύθειν, *h1rewdh-); 3 error reports. BS-164c8's incest catalogue (Eghishe ~ Eur. Andr. 174) is a striking match but a topos about Persians, not inherited.
